column2: great or the patient's condition is critical; follow local protocols.

column1: Hazmat decontamination (Packaging and aircraft safety)
column2: Ensure thoroughly decontaminated; hazardous fumes in a confined cabin can overcome the crew, and contaminated aircraft may be permanently taken out of service (some programs refuse all hazmat-exposed patients).

column1: Airway management (Packaging and aircraft safety)
column2: If possible and appropriate, manage airway with an endotracheal tube prior to aircraft arrival.

column1: Chest access (Packaging and aircraft safety)
column2: Leave the chest accessible on intubated patients so the flight crew can assess breath sounds before transport.

column1: Backboard compatibility (Packaging and aircraft safety)
column2: Verify the backboard fits the responding helicopter model.

column1: Secure patient (Packaging and aircraft safety)
column2: Firmly secure to the backboard to prevent jostling during loading and flight.

column1: Secure loose items (Packaging and aircraft safety)
column2: Tape or strap all equipment, blankets, and sheets so nothing blows into the rotor or engine; secure all loose scene equipment.

column1: Prepare the patient (Packaging and aircraft safety)
column2: Explain what you are doing and warn them about the noise and rotor wash.

column1: Protect the patient (Packaging and aircraft safety)
column2: Cover the patient's eyes, ears, and exposed wounds from noise and rotor wash.

column1: Wet the landing zone (Packaging and aircraft safety)
column2: Consider having an engine company wet down the LZ to prevent blowing dust and debris.

column1: Rescuer gear (Packaging and aircraft safety)
column2: Remove loose clothing or hats so they cannot blow into the rotor or engine.

column1: Minimize personnel (Packaging and aircraft safety)
column2: Keep the number of people under the rotors to a minimum at all times.

column1: When is the recovery position appropriate?
column2: For an appropriately breathing patient when indicated, with ongoing airway and breathing assessment; it can reduce but not eliminate aspiration risk. If breathing is absent or inadequate, prioritize resuscitation or assisted ventilation.

column1: How should children be restrained during ambulance transport?
column2: Use an agency-approved size- and weight-appropriate restraint in a permitted mounting configuration. Do not improvise with padding or assume a personal car seat is compatible; never transport a child unsecured or in an adult’s arms.

column1: Can a scoop stretcher be used for transfers involving suspected spinal injury?
column2: The historical textbook prohibition is not universal. The 2018 consensus recognizes scoop stretchers as an option to minimize motion during transfers; follow device instructions, patient tolerance and local protocol.

column1: Is the textbook’s 300-pound scoop-stretcher capacity universal?
column2: No. It is a model-specific example; verify the actual device’s rated capacity and instructions.

column1: What are the advantages and limitations of a scoop stretcher?
column2: It assembles around the patient and may fit confined areas; it requires sufficient access, personnel, padding and secure latches. Follow model-specific instructions and local protocol.

column1: What is the difference between positioning a breathing pregnant patient and managing cardiac arrest in later pregnancy?
column2: For an appropriately breathing patient, position to reduce major-vessel compression. For arrest with fundus at or above the umbilicus, the source calls for manual leftward uterine displacement with CPR, not compromising compressions by rolling her onto her side; follow protocol.
